newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Bank/Portugal does not see gold sales to reach EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bank/Portugal does not see gold sales to reach EMU.

text.p: The Bank of Portugal does not expect to sell some of its gold reserves in order to help the country to meet targets for joining a single European currency, a central bank source said.
The source told Reuters that the amounts earned from the profit on sales of part of its gold reserves would be too small to have much impact on meeting budget targets for joining the euro in 1999.
The Portuguese budget proposals, now being considered by parliament, forecast that the budget deficit will drop to 2.9 percent of Gross Domestic Product in 1997 from around four percent this year.
Prime Minister Antonio Guterres has said he was confident that Portugal would be among the first wave of countries to join the euro.

The source added that even if the central bank decided to sell part of its gold reserves next year, the profits would not show up in official statistics until 1998, just before the official launch of the single currency in January 1999.
A central bank report estimated that the reserves at the end of 1995 stood at about 500 kilos of pure gold, worth some 775 billion escudos ($5 billion).
The central bank source was speaking after Economy Minister Augusto Mateus said Portugal may sell part of its substantial gold reserves.
"Portugal, which holds a large proportion of its reserves in gold, had for some years and still has the possibility to sell part of its gold reserves," Mateus told TSF radio.

The central bank source said that published remarks by central bank governor Antonio De Sousa, who said this month that the bank had no immediate plans to sell gold to meet convergence criteria, remained valid.

De Sousa told Expresso weekly in the interview published on October 6: "The possibility to sell gold to meet Maastricht criteria does not exist as, if the operation took place in 1997 the results would only show through in 1998."
